subject: Physics
title: Vectors
learningOutcomes: Distinguish scalars from vectors, represent a vector graphically, and define the unit vector, null vector and position vector.
Define rectangular components and write a vector in the form A = Ax î + Ay ĵ.
Find the magnitudes of the rectangular components using Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A sinθ.
Find the magnitude and direction of a vector from its components using A = √(Ax² + Ay²) and θ = tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax).
Solve numerical problems on resolving a vector into components and rebuilding it from them.
Define the scalar (dot) product and state A · B = AB cosθ, including its meaning as one magnitude times the component of the other vector.
Give examples of the scalar product: work, power and electric flux.
State and explain the properties of the scalar product: commutative, results at 0°, 90° and 180°, self-product and unit-vector products.
Use the scalar product in component form, and use it to find the angle between two vectors and the projection of one on another.
Define the vector (cross) product, state A × B = AB sinθ n̂, and apply the right-hand rule to find its direction.
Give examples of the vector product: torque and angular momentum.
State and explain the properties of the vector product: anti-commutative, results at 0°, 180° and 90°, self-product and unit-vector products.
Evaluate the vector product in component form using a determinant.
Explain that |A × B| equals the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are A and B.
Compare the scalar and vector products and choose the correct one for a given physical situation.
Connect resolution, the scalar product and the vector product through the same right-angled triangle and the functions cosθ and sinθ.

sections.heading: Scalars and Vectors
sections.body: A scalar is completely described by a magnitude (a number with a unit): mass, time, length, speed, energy, work and power. A vector needs a magnitude and a direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, torque and angular momentum. A vector is drawn as an arrow whose length (to scale) shows the magnitude and whose arrowhead shows the direction. In print a vector is written in bold, or with an arrow over the letter, such as A; its magnitude is written |A| or simply A.

sections.heading: Unit Vector, Null Vector and Position Vector
sections.body: A unit vector has magnitude one and no unit; it only shows direction. The unit vector along A is Â = A/A. Along the x, y and z axes the unit vectors are î, ĵ and k̂. The null (zero) vector has zero magnitude and an arbitrary direction. The position vector r of a point P(x, y) locates it from the origin, r = x î + y ĵ, with magnitude r = √(x² + y²).

sections.heading: Rectangular Components of a Vector
sections.body: Any vector in a plane can be replaced by two perpendicular vectors along the x- and y-axes: its rectangular components Ax and Ay. Drop perpendiculars from the head of A to the two axes to form a right-angled triangle. Then A = Ax î + Ay ĵ. The components do the same job as the single vector, and because they are at right angles they do not affect each other. This is why resolving a vector makes force and motion problems easy.

sections.heading: Magnitudes of the Components
sections.body: If A makes an angle θ with the +x axis, the right-angled triangle gives cosθ = Ax/A and sinθ = Ay/A. Hence Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A sinθ. Check the extremes: at θ = 0° the vector lies along x, so Ax = A and Ay = 0; at θ = 90° it lies along y, so Ax = 0 and Ay = A. The component next to the angle uses cosine; the component opposite the angle uses sine. Signs follow the quadrant.

sections.heading: Magnitude and Direction from Components
sections.body: When Ax and Ay are known, Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle gives A² = Ax² + Ay², so A = √(Ax² + Ay²). The direction is given by tanθ = Ay/Ax, so θ = tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax). The calculator angle is measured from the x-axis; check the quadrant from the signs of Ax and Ay. Ax = Ay gives θ = 45°; Ax = 3, Ay = 4 gives A = 5 and θ = 53.1°.

sections.heading: Scalar (Dot) Product
sections.body: The scalar product of A and B is A · B = AB cosθ, where θ is the angle between them (tails joined). It is the magnitude of one vector multiplied by the component of the other along it, so A · B = (A cosθ) B = A (B cosθ). The result is a scalar. The product has its largest positive value at 0° (parallel), is zero at 90° (perpendicular) and has its largest negative value at 180° (anti-parallel).

sections.heading: Examples of the Scalar Product
sections.body: Work: W = F · d = F d cosθ; only the component of the force along the displacement does work, so a force perpendicular to the motion does none. Power: P = F · v = F v cosθ, the rate of work. Electric flux: Φ = E · A = E A cosθ, where the area vector A is normal to the surface. All three give scalar answers, and all three are largest when the two vectors are parallel.

sections.heading: Properties of the Scalar Product
sections.body: (1) A · B = B · A, the commutative property. (2) A · A = A², the square of the magnitude. (3) If A · B = 0 and neither vector is null, the vectors are perpendicular. (4) î · î = ĵ · ĵ = k̂ · k̂ = 1 and î · ĵ = ĵ · k̂ = k̂ · î = 0. (5) The scalar product is distributive: A · (B + C) = A · B + A · C. The angle between two vectors follows from cosθ = A · B/(AB).

sections.heading: Scalar Product in Component Form
sections.body: Write A = Ax î + Ay ĵ + Az k̂ and B = Bx î + By ĵ + Bz k̂. Multiplying term by term and using î · î = 1 and î · ĵ = 0 leaves only the like-axis terms: A · B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz. The component of A along B is (A · B)/B. To find the angle, compute A · B, A and B, then use cosθ = (A · B)/(AB).

sections.heading: Vector (Cross) Product
sections.body: The vector product of A and B is A × B = AB sinθ n̂, where θ is the angle between them and n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B. The result is a vector. Its magnitude AB sinθ is largest (AB) at 90° and zero at 0° and 180°. Its direction follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand from the first vector A toward the second vector B through the smaller angle; the erect thumb points along A × B.

sections.heading: Examples of the Vector Product
sections.body: Torque: τ = r × F, with magnitude rF sinθ; it is the turning effect of a force about a point and is zero when the force acts along the line of r. Angular momentum: L = r × p = m (r × v). Both are vectors perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors in the product, with direction found by the right-hand rule. The magnitude of a vector product also gives the area of a parallelogram.

sections.heading: Properties of the Vector Product
sections.body: (1) A × B = −(B × A): the product is anti-commutative, so reversing the order reverses the direction. (2) A × A = 0, and the product vanishes for parallel and anti-parallel vectors. (3) For perpendicular vectors |A × B| = AB. (4) î × î = ĵ × ĵ = k̂ × k̂ = 0. (5) î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ, and the reversed orders give the negatives.

sections.heading: Vector Product in Component Form
sections.body: The vector product of A = Ax î + Ay ĵ + Az k̂ and B = Bx î + By ĵ + Bz k̂ is the determinant with rows î ĵ k̂, Ax Ay Az and Bx By Bz. Expanding gives A × B = (AyBz − AzBy) î − (AxBz − AzBx) ĵ + (AxBy − AyBx) k̂. For two vectors in the x–y plane only the k̂ term survives: A × B = (AxBy − AyBx) k̂. Remember the minus sign before the ĵ term.

sections.heading: Area of a Parallelogram and a Triangle
sections.body: Place two vectors A and B tail to tail; they are the adjacent sides of a parallelogram. Its height is B sinθ, so its area is base × height = AB sinθ = |A × B|. The triangle formed by the same two vectors has half that area, ½ |A × B|. Because the area equals a vector product, parallel vectors give zero area (the shape collapses).

sections.heading: Dot Product versus Cross Product
sections.body: Both products use the angle between the vectors, but through different functions. The dot product uses cosθ, gives a scalar, and measures how much the vectors point the same way (zero when perpendicular). The cross product uses sinθ, gives a vector, and measures how much they point apart (zero when parallel). Together, (A · B)² + |A × B|² = A²B² and tanθ = |A × B|/(A · B).

definitions.definition: A physical quantity described completely by a magnitude (a number with a unit), for example mass, time, work.
A physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction, for example force, displacement, torque.
A vector of magnitude one with no unit that shows direction only; Â = A/A, and î, ĵ, k̂ along the axes.
A vector of zero magnitude and arbitrary direction.
The vector drawn from the origin to a point P(x, y): r = x î + y ĵ.
The two mutually perpendicular vectors Ax î and Ay ĵ into which a vector can be resolved.
Splitting a vector into two perpendicular components: Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A sinθ.
A = √(Ax² + Ay²) for a vector with rectangular components Ax and Ay.
The angle θ with the +x axis found from tanθ = Ay/Ax.
A · B = AB cosθ; the result is a scalar.
The scalar product of force and displacement, W = F · d = F d cosθ (unit: joule).
The scalar product of force and velocity, P = F · v = F v cosθ (unit: watt).
The scalar product of the electric field and the area vector, Φ = E · A = E A cosθ.
The component of A along B, equal to A cosθ = (A · B)/B.
A × B = AB sinθ n̂; the result is a vector perpendicular to both A and B.
Curl the fingers of the right hand from the first vector toward the second through the smaller angle; the thumb shows the direction of A × B.
The vector product of position vector and force, τ = r × F, with magnitude rF sinθ (unit: N m).
The vector product of position vector and linear momentum, L = r × p.
The order does not matter: A · B = B · A holds for the dot product but not for the cross product.
Reversing the order reverses the sign: A × B = −(B × A).
The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides A and B is |A × B| = AB sinθ.
Two non-null vectors at 90° to each other; their scalar product is zero.
Two non-null vectors at 0° or 180° to each other; their vector product is zero.

examTips: Before using Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A sinθ, check which axis the angle is measured from; if it is measured from the y-axis, the sine and cosine swap.
For θ = tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax) always look at the signs of Ax and Ay to place the vector in the correct quadrant before writing the final angle.
Write the scalar product as A · B and the vector product as A × B; never use the wrong symbol, because an examiner marks the type of the answer (a number or a vector).
A · B uses cosθ and gives a number; A × B uses sinθ and gives a vector. In any long answer say this in one line.
For the direction of A × B, name the right-hand rule and state it fully: fingers from A to B through the smaller angle, thumb along A × B.
In the determinant for A × B, the ĵ term has a minus sign: (AyBz − AzBy) î − (AxBz − AzBx) ĵ + (AxBy − AyBx) k̂.
Remember the three special results: A · B = 0 for perpendicular vectors, A × B = 0 for parallel and anti-parallel vectors, and A × A = 0.
Learn the unit-vector table: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ (cyclic order is positive); reversing the order gives the negative.
Give the area of a parallelogram as |A × B| = AB sinθ and the area of a triangle as ½ |A × B|; a missing half is a common lost mark.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is a vector quantity?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Force has direction as well as magnitude, so it is a vector; mass, time and work are scalars.

options: Magnitude 1 and a unit of metre

practiceQuestions.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude one and no unit; it only shows direction.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A force of 10 N acts at 30° with the horizontal. Which expression gives its vertical component?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The vertical component is opposite the angle, so Fy = F sinθ = 10 sin30° = 5 N.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A rope pulls a box with 40 N at 60° to the floor. What is the horizontal component of the pull?
The components of a force are Fx = 12 N and Fy = 5 N. The magnitude of the force is:
A force of 20 N moves a body 5 m in its own direction. The work done is:

practiceQuestions.explanation: Cyclic order î → ĵ → k̂ gives î × ĵ = k̂.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which product is zero for two perpendicular vectors?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A · B = AB cos90° = 0, while |A × B| = AB sin90° = AB.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Work is a scalar quantity even though it is calculated from two vectors.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Work is the scalar (dot) product of force and displacement, and its result is a number.

practiceQuestions.prompt: If θ = 0° with the x-axis, the y-component of the vector is zero.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Ay = A sin0° = 0, so the vector lies entirely along the x-axis.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A × B = B × A for any two vectors.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The vector product is anti-commutative: A × B = −(B × A).

practiceQuestions.prompt: If A · B = 0 for two non-null vectors, then the vectors are perpendicular.
The scalar product of two vectors is also called the ______ product.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The scalar product is written with a dot, A · B, so it is also called the dot product.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The direction of the vector product is found by the ______ rule.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The right-hand rule gives the direction of A × B.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The magnitude of a vector with components 3 and 4 is ______.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps of finding the magnitude and direction of a vector from its components, starting with writing the components.

items: Write the given Ax and Ay
Take tan⁻¹ to get the angle θ
Take the square root to get A
correctOrder: Write the given Ax and Ay
Take the square root to get A
Take tan⁻¹ to get the angle θ

sequencingActivity.explanation: The magnitude comes first from Pythagoras, then the direction from the tangent ratio; both use the same two components.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Find the angle between A = 6î + 8ĵ and B = 3î − 4ĵ.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: A · B = (6)(3) + (8)(−4) = −14, A = 10 and B = 5, so cosθ = −14/50 = −0.28 and θ = 106.3°. (73.7° is the supplement, found if the sign of A · B is ignored.)

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A force F = 4î + 3ĵ N moves a body from the point (1, 2) m to the point (7, 10) m. Find the work done.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Displacement d = (7 − 1)î + (10 − 2)ĵ = 6î + 8ĵ m. W = F · d = (4)(6) + (3)(8) = 48 J. (50 J is F × d, found by ignoring the angle.)

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A force F = 4î − 5ĵ N acts at the position r = 2î + 3ĵ m. Find the torque τ = r × F.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Both vectors lie in the x–y plane, so τ = (rxFy − ryFx) k̂ = (2)(−5) − (3)(4) = −10 − 12 = −22, i.e. τ = −22 k̂ N m.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: For two vectors, A · B = 12 and |A × B| = 12√3. Find the angle between them and the product AB of their magnitudes.
Find the area of the triangle whose adjacent sides are A = 2î + 3ĵ + k̂ and B = î − ĵ + 2k̂.
